title: DreamVLA: From Generated Human Motions to Humanoid Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies typically depends on substantial robot demonstration data, making human teleoperation a costly and cumbersome bottleneck, particularly for whole-body humanoid interaction. Reinforcement learning in simulation offers an alternative for scaling this data, but designing task-specific rewards remains challenging.

extra.comment: Accepted to CoRL 2026 workshops G2A: From Generative Models to Robot Actions and Open Problems in Contact-Rich Loco-Manipulation
extra.full_text: Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies typically depends on substantial robot demonstration data, making human teleoperation a costly and cumbersome bottleneck, particularly for whole-body humanoid interaction. Reinforcement learning in simulation offers an alternative for scaling this data, but designing task-specific rewards remains challenging. To address this, we propose DreamVLA, which uses generated motion trajectories to guide reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation, converting them into reliable task execution trajectories. These trajectories train VLA models in simulation without new task-specific teleoperation data. Our central contribution is a reference-conditioned DAgger distillation procedure: after a failed learner rollout, we restart the RL expert from a sampled learner state with the same reference suffix and aggregate successful corrective trajectories, addressing the distribution shift left by offline imitation. We evaluate picking from a platform, opening a drawer, pressing a button, and walking and picking from a platform, with ablations of DAgger iterations, residual RL, and generated dataset scale. Project website: ember-center-berkeley.github.io/DreamVLA.

title: Zero-Shot VLA Adaptation with Retrieved Guidance
summary: Pre-training large parametric "Vision-Language-Action" (VLA) models on large demonstration datasets has recently yielded promising results for general-purpose manipulation. However, these models still struggle under even small domain shifts relative to the training data, such as changes in camera viewpoint, background, object identity, or robot morphology.

extra.full_text: Pre-training large parametric "Vision-Language-Action" (VLA) models on large demonstration datasets has recently yielded promising results for general-purpose manipulation. However, these models still struggle under even small domain shifts relative to the training data, such as changes in camera viewpoint, background, object identity, or robot morphology. Motivated by the success of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in language models, we pursue retrieval to boost VLA performance. Specifically, we seek to leverage retrieval from domain-mismatched, "in-the-wild" demonstration datasets like DROID to guide a VLA's behavior in a new target domain. To achieve this, we introduce RAGu, which overcomes robotics-specific challenges for RAG: (1) It incorporates simple geometric calibration to transform source demonstrations into the target setup and reduce cross-domain differences. (2) It uses a coarse-to-fine retrieval strategy that selects, from a large pool of pre-warped candidates, the trajectory most compatible with the base VLA. (3) It guides the VLA's flow-matching inference procedure rather than seeking to retrain the base model or expand its limited context window. We evaluate RAGu across real-world, simulation, sim-to-real transfer, and cross-embodiment humanoid manipulation. We find it improves real-world VLA success rates from 20% to 80% and outperforms the closest-related baselines in sim. Project website: raguvla.github.io

title: DobotTrack: Target-Grounded Vision-Language-Action Learning for Embodied Person Tracking
summary: Language-guided embodied person tracking requires a mobile agent to identify a target from a referring description and consistently follow the target under egocentric observations. We present DobotTrack, a target-grounded vision-language-action (VLA) framework that integrates auxiliary grounding supervision with efficient temporal modeling.

extra.full_text: Language-guided embodied person tracking requires a mobile agent to identify a target from a referring description and consistently follow the target under egocentric observations. We present DobotTrack, a target-grounded vision-language-action (VLA) framework that integrates auxiliary grounding supervision with efficient temporal modeling. We systematically investigate five auxiliary tasks---person segmentation, bounding-box grounding, visual-spatial classification (VSC), future DINO feature prediction, and future-frame prediction---and adopt complementary mask and bounding-box supervision to enhance target delineation and localization. We introduce Q-identity, a target-conditioned historical visual compression module that leverages target-grounding predictions to selectively preserve identity-discriminative appearance features and spatial cues in compact historical tokens. On EVT-Bench, our 0.8B-parameter model achieves an average success rate of 77.9%, exceeding OmTrackVLA by 16.9 percentage points across the three tasks. We further construct a real-world person-tracking dataset collected using a quadruped robot, comprising 126 episodes and 596,323 mask-annotated frames. The target masks enable automatic derivation of bounding boxes and visual-spatial labels encoding horizontal position and apparent image scale, providing additional grounding supervision without separate manual annotation of these labels. Together, our framework and annotation pipeline support learning target-grounded tracking policies from simulated and real-world data. Code is available at https://github.com/Dobot-Team/dobot_track.

title: VICTR: Value-Informed In-Context Learning for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Recent advances in robot foundation models have highlighted the potential of in-context learning (ICL) for adapting robot behavior from demonstrations without further fine-tuning.

extra.comment: 11 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Project page: https://ai4ce.github.io/VICTR/
extra.full_text: Recent advances in robot foundation models have highlighted the potential of in-context learning (ICL) for adapting robot behavior from demonstrations without further fine-tuning. Previous work has used retrieval-based post-training to equip pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models with the capability for ICL by teaching them to condition action predictions on retrieved visually-relevant demonstration chunks. However, the effectiveness of retrieval hinges on selecting context relevant to the current execution stage, which visual similarity alone may not capture. We introduce VICTR, a framework enabling in-context learning in VLAs via progress-informed context retrieval built around an In-Context Value Function Estimator (IC-VFE). IC-VFE conditions on a reference demonstration video, a language instruction and the current observation to estimate task-relative progress. By conditioning progress estimation on a reference demonstration, IC-VFE can align the current state with a demonstrated execution even for tasks unseen during training. VICTR uses the estimated progress to select demonstration chunks at corresponding stages of execution and supplies them to a $π_{0.5}$ policy post-trained for in-context action generation. On unseen out-of-domain real-world manipulation tasks, VICTR raises the success rate from 6.2% for a fine-tuned $π_{0.5}$ baseline to 23.8% and more than doubles the task progress rate, from 28.9% to 55.5%. Project page with code, data and videos: https://ai4ce.github.io/VICTR/

title: Spatial Representation Distillation and Knowledge Routing for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Understanding three-dimensional physical structure has become essential for vision-language-action models (VLAs). However, existing approaches either rely on explicit geometric inputs at inference time or adopt a single visual pathway, potentially compromising the visual-semantic knowledge inherited from pre-trained models.

extra.full_text: Understanding three-dimensional physical structure has become essential for vision-language-action models (VLAs). However, existing approaches either rely on explicit geometric inputs at inference time or adopt a single visual pathway, potentially compromising the visual-semantic knowledge inherited from pre-trained models. We present SPARK-VLA, Spatial Representation distillation and Knowledge routing for VLAs, a preserve-specialize-route framework for spatially adapting VLAs without requiring external 3D inputs or experts at inference. SPARK-VLA consists of two key components: (1) spatial representation distillation, which transfers 3D understanding from a frozen 3D expert to a LoRA-adapted visual branch by aligning attention responses while preserving the original visual pathway, and (2) a lightweight knowledge router, which selectively forwards action-relevant visual tokens to the language model using routing supervision derived from action-loss gradients. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and real-world manipulation, SPARK-VLA achieves strong performance with only a 0.5B language backbone and approximately 53M trainable parameters, providing an effective and parameter-efficient approach to 3D-aware VLA learning. Code is available at https://github.com/park-jungin/spark-vla.

title: SUGARv2: Learning Diverse Visual Humanoid Loco-Manipulation Skills from Synthesized Interaction References
summary: Scaling up visual humanoid loco-manipulation skill acquisition requires reducing the human effort needed as tasks and spatial configurations expand, particularly in demonstration collection and task-specific training design.

extra.full_text: Scaling up visual humanoid loco-manipulation skill acquisition requires reducing the human effort needed as tasks and spatial configurations expand, particularly in demonstration collection and task-specific training design. We present SUGARv2, a unified framework for learning diverse visual humanoid loco-manipulation skills through interaction reference synthesis and a shared training pipeline. To obtain diverse references at low cost, we adapt reusable task templates to different spatial configurations, synthesizing coordinated robot and object motions. To reduce task-specific reward design and training effort, we use reference-based imitation as a common learning objective across tasks. We first train privileged teachers to execute these references, then train visual policies through teacher distillation and reinforcement learning with the same reference-based mimic rewards, using diverse object instances and visual domain randomization to support visual generalization and sim-to-real transfer. Across five humanoid loco-manipulation tasks, SUGARv2 achieves a mean success rate of 91.0% in simulation. Deployment on a real humanoid robot further demonstrates successful sim-to-real transfer for whole-body manipulation. These results demonstrate the framework's potential for learning diverse visual humanoid loco-manipulation skills.

title: STRIDE: Learning Humanoid Locomotion in Minutes with Acceleration-Based Rewards
summary: Learning locomotion directly on a humanoid robot is a promising direction to avoid the sim-to-real gap. However, locomotion rewards in Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically track the base velocity, which cannot be measured onboard without an external motion capture system or well-calibrated state estimator.

extra.full_text: Learning locomotion directly on a humanoid robot is a promising direction to avoid the sim-to-real gap. However, locomotion rewards in Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically track the base velocity, which cannot be measured onboard without an external motion capture system or well-calibrated state estimator. This is why we introduce \method{}, which learns humanoid locomotion from minutes of samples with a reward that only requires the onboard Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU). Instead of tracking the base velocity, STRIDE rewards the robot for following a commanded acceleration profile. To learn efficiently from this reward, we use the off-policy RL algorithm XQC and combine a high gain setting for the joint position controllers with left-right symmetry augmentation. In simulation, STRIDE learns to walk on the Unitree G1 and Booster T1 humanoids within 14 minutes of samples. Compared to learning without these two components, it reduces the falls during training by 81%, while without them the robot learns only in over an hour.

title: It Takes Two to Tangram: Multi-Agent Object Centric Reinforcement Learning for Assembly
summary: Geometric assembly requires fine spatiotemporal coordination to place parts without causing collisions or deadlocks under tight clearances. To address this, we present an object-centric reinforcement learning framework that treats each part as an agent and learns a shared policy for continuous assembly control.

extra.comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
extra.full_text: Geometric assembly requires fine spatiotemporal coordination to place parts without causing collisions or deadlocks under tight clearances. To address this, we present an object-centric reinforcement learning framework that treats each part as an agent and learns a shared policy for continuous assembly control. A graph neural network represents the pieces, their target poses, and their spatial relationships, and predicts translational and angular velocities for each component. Per-agent proximal policy optimization with a centralized graph critic directly learns motion and temporal coordination within a single feedback policy. extra.full_text: Most robotic handwriting rigidly mounts the pen and reduces writing to trajectory tracking. A freely held pen instead couples grasp stability, tip motion, and contact force. We present Grip, Trace, Write, a force-aware simulation environment and learning framework for high-DoF handwriting. A two-branch actor separates pen retention from arm-wrist writing while preserving their closed-loop coupling. Training learns a grasp controller, initializes writing from inverse-kinematics demonstrations by behavior cloning, and improves writing through reinforcement learning with rewards on ink, force, time, and retention. Across diverse tasks, the policy improves completion, precision, force regulation, and efficiency over behavior cloning and inverse kinematics, and generalizes without fine-tuning to unseen English and Chinese content. These results establish force-aware handwriting as a testbed for dexterous tool use.

title: SURE:Spatiotemporal Uncertainty Representation for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Learning
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have become a promising paradigm for end-to-end robot control, but their effectiveness still depends heavily on large volumes of demonstration data.

extra.full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have become a promising paradigm for end-to-end robot control, but their effectiveness still depends heavily on large volumes of demonstration data. In manipulation tasks, this dependence is compounded by structured spatiotemporal uncertainty in the action space: multiple nearby actions or trajectories may successfully solve the same task, while semantically equivalent demonstrations often unfold at different speeds. Standard pointwise supervision treats each demonstrated action as an exact target, imposing an unnecessary learning burden under such uncertainty. We present SURE, a data-efficient VLA training framework that explicitly models both spatial and temporal uncertainty. SURE augments a VLA backbone with a lightweight transposed-convolutional probabilistic action decoder that captures spatial uncertainty through local correlations among neighboring action bins. It further introduces Soft-DTW alignment supervision to accommodate local timing variations between predicted and demonstrated action chunks. Together, these two components reduce sensitivity to demonstrator-specific poses and execution timing, enabling more data-efficient action learning. We evaluate SURE on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation tasks. Even with only 10% of the demonstration data or 20% of the training steps, SURE achieves manipulation success rates that match or surpass baseline VLAs.

title: Autonomous Particle Image Velocimetry Using Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Reinforcement Learning
summary: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) reconstructs a flow field from the motion of tracer particles but the reconstruction quality is bounded by how well the flow structure of interest is resolved in the images. The acquisition position is typically fixed by the operator before the measurement.

extra.full_text: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) reconstructs a flow field from the motion of tracer particles but the reconstruction quality is bounded by how well the flow structure of interest is resolved in the images. The acquisition position is typically fixed by the operator before the measurement. We cast camera placement as a sequential decision-making problem and train a reinforcement learning agent to control a 6-DoF manipulator equipped with a camera, enabling it to locate, frame and resolve a hydrofoil wake in a water tunnel. The agent commands the camera pose and observes the scene only through the velocity field and uncertainty estimated from time-separated image pairs. It is trained entirely in a photorealistic simulation of our water tunnel, with wakes generated by Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations of hydrofoils with varying profiles, positions and angles of attack. After zero-shot transfer to the real water tunnel, the policy reliably locates and frames the wakes of randomly placed hydrofoils. It resolves the wake at a higher resolution than a fixed camera view and with lower error in the measured flow statistics, in roughly half the time of a full scan and with far fewer image pairs.

title: ForPC: Force-Aware Whole-Body Control for Precise Humanoid Cart Pushing
summary: Humanoid robots are expected to take over strenuous material handling in manufacturing, logistics, and healthcare, where operating existing wheeled carts would let them move heavy loads without modifying the workplace.

extra.comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Project website: https://roboforpc.github.io/. Corresponding author: Cheng Cheng
extra.full_text: Humanoid robots are expected to take over strenuous material handling in manufacturing, logistics, and healthcare, where operating existing wheeled carts would let them move heavy loads without modifying the workplace. However, humanoid cart pushing remains challenging because the bimanual grasp closes a force-coupled loop in which the contact wrenches that drive the cart also disturb the robot's balance, and payload changes alter the coupled dynamics. We propose ForPC, a force-aware whole-body control framework that regulates cart velocity through two-stage reinforcement learning. A locomotion prior is first trained under varied hand loads and upper-body postures to provide balance support. A force latent and a state latent are then inferred from onboard observations, without external force sensors, and fed to a residual policy that coordinates bounded arm, waist, and leg adjustments with base-velocity commands. Multi-objective rewards penalize bimanual internal opposition, grasp slip, and actuator saturation, encouraging the policy to apply contact force on demand without human demonstrations. Sim-to-sim experiments show that ForPC reduces cart-velocity RMSE by up to 68.2% relative to a locomotion-only baseline (Loco-only) and cross-track RMSE by up to 74.2% on the multi-bend route. Trained solely in simulation, the policy also transfers to a physical Unitree G1 without real-world training or fine-tuning and, with no payload-specific adjustment, pushes a cart carrying up to 30 kg at 0.5 m/s. These results suggest that humanoid robots could eventually replace humans for efficient material handling in daily life.

title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
summary: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs).

extra.full_text: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.

title: Encoding Memory in World Models with Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
summary: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning.

extra.full_text: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning. In this work, we address the problem of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. We introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode observations into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark. Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.

title: DKWBC: Decoupling Motion Tracking and Balancing for Humanoid Whole-Body Control
summary: Humanoid whole-body control requires a robot to track diverse reference motions while maintaining balance under gravity, torque limits, contact switching, and external disturbances. Existing reinforcement-learning-based trackers typically learn control outputs that jointly address motion tracking and balance.

extra.full_text: Humanoid whole-body control requires a robot to track diverse reference motions while maintaining balance under gravity, torque limits, contact switching, and external disturbances. Existing reinforcement-learning-based trackers typically learn control outputs that jointly address motion tracking and balance. However, similar reference poses can correspond to substantially different dynamic demands, requiring a unified policy to learn motion-dependent control requirements alongside balance corrections. This can complicate learning and lead to high-frequency fluctuations in control outputs. We propose DKWBC, a dynamics-informed whole-body control framework that combines explicit model-based tracking with a learned balancing residual. Inspired by the model-based and environmental-wrench contributions to joint torques in floating-base dynamics, DKWBC uses inverse-dynamics feedforward and joint PD feedback to supply tracking torques, while a residual policy learns additional joint-torque corrections for balanced execution. By explicitly accounting for motion-dependent torque demands, this structure simplifies the policy's learning task. Experiments in simulation and on real hardware demonstrate that a single learned balancing policy generalizes across motion datasets while maintaining accurate motion tracking and balance across ground support, attached payloads, and physical interaction. title: VLA Handover: Failure-Prediction-Based Switching from On-Robot to Server VLA Models
summary: Large vision-language-action (VLA) models generalize well but are difficult to run in real time on a robot, and small VLAs that run there fail more often. Remote inference over beyond-5G and 6G networks lets a robot use a large VLA on a server, but querying the server for every action chunk limits the number of robots per server.

extra.full_text: Large vision-language-action (VLA) models generalize well but are difficult to run in real time on a robot, and small VLAs that run there fail more often. Remote inference over beyond-5G and 6G networks lets a robot use a large VLA on a server, but querying the server for every action chunk limits the number of robots per server. We propose VLA handover: the robot runs a small VLA (S-VLA) and switches to a large VLA (L-VLA) on a server only when the S-VLA is likely to fail. We formulate the switching as minimizing the request cost under a required success probability and, since this problem cannot be solved directly, propose a heuristic framework that retrains neither VLA. In simulation with SmolVLA and $π_{0.5}$ on three of the four LIBERO suites, VLA handover raised the success rate by 11-22 percentage points over the S-VLA alone and sent 49-77% fewer requests than server-only control at a 2-4 percentage-point lower success rate, and its completion time grew less with the network latency.

title: Can Agentic Robotics Solve Robotics’ Data Scaling Problem?
summary: Robotics companies are investing heavily in the belief that data will solve the most difficult problems in robotics. Once AI systems have ingested enough data from human demonstrations, the thinking goes, robots will be able to perform the vast majority of the manual tasks that humans now do.

extra.full_text: Robotics companies are investing heavily in the belief that data will solve the most difficult problems in robotics. Once AI systems have ingested enough data from human demonstrations, the thinking goes, robots will be able to perform the vast majority of the manual tasks that humans now do. There are even robotics companies that exist solely to collect training data and sell it to other robotics companies in pursuit of this goal. But whether data will finally bring us general-purpose robots is an open question . Nobody knows how much data would be necessary , what kind of data is important , or whether something else might be missing . And there are other problems with a reliance on massive amounts of data: the resulting AI algorithms are essentially black boxes, which despite their high performance are difficult or impossible for humans to understand. This characteristic is becoming increasingly concerning in commercial deployments, where robots must be flexible, reliable, and safe. At the 2026 Conference on Robot Learning this week, UC Berkeley and NVIDIA are jointly announcing a new approach to using AI to program robots for everyday practical tasks in industrial environments. Called agentic robotics, this technique leverages the latest advances in AI coding tools while in some sense bringing robotics back to its roots—achieving a fundamental understanding of how a robot works, and then writing human-readable code to get it to do useful things, no data (and no humans) required. The Data Problem For decades, robots were programmed with model-based methods, meaning that their behavior was based on a detailed understanding (or model) of the physics and mathematics underlying the robot and its environment. Roboticists would first develop these models, and then write painstakingly detailed code telling their robots how to act. The resulting hand-tuned robotic systems could operate fast and reliably, but this approach has fallen out of favor because it requires both human time and human expertise. It’s much easier to just feed a huge amount of human demonstration data into a machine-learning system, and the results that come out are both adaptable and reliable—up to a point. “The imitation learning paradigm has hit a plateau,” explains Ken Goldberg , a professor of robotics at UC Berkeley whose lab is presenting a paper on agentic robotics at this week’s conference. “It’s promising for things like home robots, where speed and reliability are less of an issue. But for industrial applications, it’s very hard to get the reliability that industry requires.” Goldberg, who is also a co-founder of the industrial robotics company Ambi Robotics , has experienced this problem firsthand, as have other companies that he’s been working with, including Siemens and Bosch. “You get good performance from data initially, but then things go wrong. So you start giving it more data. But then other things go wrong. It’s not clear that adding more data is going to get you there.” The hope, according to Goldberg, is that with enough data, robots will somehow just start to work reliably, since that was the case with ChatGPT. “That’s what people have been counting on, and why investors are pouring money into these companies,” says Goldberg. “But everybody’s getting a little nervous that we haven’t hit that convergence point.” How Agentic Robotics Works The reason why language models like ChatGPT are so successful is that they can train on data at the scale of the Internet. There is no dataset for robotics that approaches that scale, and while robotics companies are desperately attempting to generate the data that they think they need, it’s a slow, expensive process. Agentic robotics, a term popularized by Goldberg along with Spencer Huang , Director of Product for Robotics at NVIDIA, is an attempt to turn programming robots from a data problem into a coding problem, which can directly leverage the scale of language models. “This is really something that’s accelerated in the past year,” Goldberg says. “The quality of agentic coding has become so good that using them to write code for robots is now viable.” Because agentic robotics is based on LLMs, it’s easy to use—you can use natural language to tell the robot what to do. One example used by the UC Berkeley researchers was asking a robotic arm to pack groceries into a bag. First, this relatively complex (to a robot) task is decomposed into simpler sub-tasks, each of them assigned to a separate coding agent. In LLM-based software, a coding agent is an autonomous AI system that can plan, write, test, and modify software with minimal human intervention. You might have one individual agent tasked with perception to identify the groceries and the bag, a second focused on object manipulation with the arm’s gripper, and a third working on transporting objects with the arm once they’ve been grasped. “We have all these robotics tools we’ve been building for the last couple decades,” explains Huang. “The problem was that a human had to go and write the code themselves. But object classifiers, pose estimation, task and motion planning, trajectory generation—everything is already there.” The coding agents can directly leverage all of that existing data contained within their language models to generate code of their own, tailored to their specific tasks. Solving the Simulation Bottleneck Once the agents have a plausible framework, they run their code in a simulation and see what happens, much like a human would. They can change starting conditions, identify failures, refine the code, and keep iterating until they’ve got a successful program. Of course, code that works in simulation can only ever be as versatile and reliable as the simulation is. “Simulations are non-trivial to build,” Goldberg explains. The more accurate the simulation has the potential to be, the more parameters there are that need to be configured to achieve and maintain that accuracy, typically by a human on a task-by-task basis. Goldberg decided to try giving an AI agent direct access to these simulation parameters, and instructing it to match the simulation to a video of the real world. “It gave us goosebumps. It was matching the whole environment, the lighting, the background, all these things that are super tedious to do. We would never have done that, but the agent did. Side by side, it was very hard to tell the difference between the simulation and the video.” Nevertheless, no matter how good a simulated environment looks, navigating the gap between that environment and the real world is still an unsolved challenge for the robotics community, says Torsten Kroeger , chief science officer at Alphabet’s Intrinsic . Kroeger, who is not directly involved in this research, continued: “I’m saying this respectfully, but there’s just no physics engine out there that can accurately model physical contact with the world.” But as with a team of human coders, the agents can troubleshoot when things inevitably don’t work quite right. The agents’ ability to work on the simulation itself offers significant advantages, because the agents can be fed video of a failed task with the goal of updating the simulation to match, while the coding agents then iterate to fix the problem. As with anything done by AI, Huang is well aware that agents writing code for robots will have their flaws. “We all know that AI agents can create slop,” Huang says. “In order to counter that, we use adversarial agent setups—where one agent designs something and another agent tries to rip it apart and find flaws.” In UC Berkeley’s testing , agentic robotics approaches were able to reach success rates of up to 99 percent, matching human hand-engineered performance, even in tasks where baseline imitation learning techniques saw success rates of only 20 percent. But as Goldberg points out, agentic robotics is not just about performance, but also about efficiency and safety. “You’re using an off the shelf coding agent. You don’t need to collect any data. And the agent is generating code that you can actually understand and fix if necessary.” Real World Agentic Robotics In the immediate future, the sweet spot for practical agentic robotics will be industrial manufacturing and manipulation tasks that require robust precision and accuracy , says Huang. “Right now, some of our partners in the semiconductor space need to place components within 0.3 mm. There’s no way you’re going to get something like GR00T [NVIDIA’s humanoid development platform] to do that today with any semblance of repeatability and robustness. What you get with agentic robotics is near-term applications.” But the real value, Huang says, is in adapting to change. “At Wistron in Taiwan [which manufactures baseboards for NVIDIA GPUs], every time they add a new product, it takes a minimum of 8 hours to retask one robot. With agentic robotics, retasking takes a minute or two instead.” Moving agentic robotics beyond these fairly well-constrained use cases may be difficult, but Huang sees this technique as a gateway towards more complex tasks. “Agentic robotics can generate tons of good quality robotic code, which is data that we can use for training the next model.” Such code generation is only an iterative step towards a general purpose capability, but Huang believes that agentic robotics may help redefine the very meaning of general intelligence in the context of robotics. “My thesis is that general intelligence for robotics will first come in the form of an agent orchestrating a mix of conventional technologies and specialized policies. To a human, it looks like general intelligence because the agent is coordinating everything under the hood.” Intrinsic’s Kroeger is more cautious about placing trust in agents. “In the context of safety and security, how do we know that these agents are really doing the right thing all the time? It’s the alignment problem . A human engineer can review everything, but the challenge will be once we start putting our trust in these agents. I can imagine that this will become a relevant conversation for the industry.” For now, Goldberg is focused on working with real companies to put agentic robotics into practice. A series of benchmarks for agentic robotics developed with NVIDIA Isaac Lab-Arena and the Newton physics engine will help researchers evaluate agent performance. “I don’t want to say that we have the solution, but I’m very excited about it,” he says. Adds Huang: “It’s a pivotal change in the way we’re doing things.”

title: The World Model Planning Accelerator (WMPA): Hardware-Algorithm Co-Design for Embedded AI in Robotics
summary: Embedded AI is moving from perception to prediction. Robots now use world models$\unicode{x2014}$learned simulators that predict the outcome of candidate actions in a compressed latent space before any is executed.

extra.full_text: Embedded AI is moving from perception to prediction. Robots now use world models$\unicode{x2014}$learned simulators that predict the outcome of candidate actions in a compressed latent space before any is executed. Every predicted step must be computed on board within a tight power and thermal budget, yet the energy these steps fundamentally require, and how far real hardware sits from it, have not been characterized. We derive lower bounds on the arithmetic operations and the CMOS dynamic energy of a latent state transition from information theory and Boolean circuit complexity. Profiling a DreamerV3-style Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM) shows that every rollout operation is memory-bandwidth bound and that a GPU consumes at least $5.9\times10^{10}$ times the CMOS energy floor. Transient 3D thermal simulations show that this inefficiency is also a thermal one, since sustained back-to-back planning heats a millimeter-scale silicon tile to 556 K even behind an ideal copper heat spreader. Guided by this chain from bound to bottleneck, we propose the World Model Planning Accelerator (WMPA), a chip architecture for embedded world model planning that combines near-memory computation, real-time entropy estimation, variable-precision rollout units, and copy-on-write latent scratchpads. With a design target of 40x lower power, the same tile stays near ambient at 306 K in simulation, pointing toward practical planning on thermally constrained robots.

title: HiMEM: Hippocampus-Inspired Memory Consolidation, Pruning, and Composition for Vision-Language-Action Models in 3D Scenes
summary: Memory plays a crucial role in long-horizon task execution and cross-task generalization for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models operating in complex 3D scenes.

extra.full_text: Memory plays a crucial role in long-horizon task execution and cross-task generalization for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models operating in complex 3D scenes. However, existing VLA memory mechanisms suffer from memory noise, particularly in complex 3D scenes, as stored episodic memories contain extensive redundant details about scene layouts, object configurations, and robot-specific states, which obscure generalizable manipulation principles and hinder cross-task transfer. To address this challenge, we first introduce a hippocampus-inspired memory consolidation mechanism that synthesizes extensive episodic experiences into a compact set of essential semantic memories, enabling VLA models to derive generalizable principles from practical experience. Second, we propose an episodic memory pruning mechanism that removes redundant episodic memories whose contents are captured by consolidated semantic memories, thereby increasing effective memory capacity and improving long-horizon task execution. Finally, to handle complex task scenarios, we develop a flexible memory composition mechanism that jointly leverages multiple episodic and semantic memories to enhance cross-scenario generalization. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus demonstrate the effectiveness of HiMEM across different VLA backbones, improving the average success rate of pi_0 from 91.88% to 98.20% on LIBERO.

title: PRISM: Primitive Routing via In-context Skill Mixing for Retentive VLA Adaptation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models promise a single language-conditioned policy adaptable to many manipulation behaviors, yet deployment additionally requires skill retention and long-horizon composition: a policy must retain previously acquired skills and reuse them inside composite tasks whose behavior changes across phases.

extra.comment: 19 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
extra.full_text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models promise a single language-conditioned policy adaptable to many manipulation behaviors, yet deployment additionally requires skill retention and long-horizon composition: a policy must retain previously acquired skills and reuse them inside composite tasks whose behavior changes across phases. The standard recipe absorbs every new task into one shared update, which provides neither a parameter-level locus for reusable skills nor a mechanism for invoking each skill along the trajectory. We observe that this missing structure is latent rather than absent: per-skill low-rank updates of a pretrained VLA occupy a robustly distinguishable, low-dimensional subspace, and a single composite-task LoRA concentrates roughly half of its Frobenius energy in this subspace, against a near-zero matched random-rotation control. Building on this geometry, we introduce PRISM, which represents reusable skills as parameter-level primitives: each skill family is stored as a dedicated low-rank action-expert adapter in a primitive bank, primitives are augmented with skill-specific low-rank residuals and composed at inference by a per-chunk VLM-conditioned router that reads the prefix representation to track task progress, and the router is supervised by per-chunk labels from a deterministic, task-conditioned, action-derived oracle. During composite training, the vision encoder, the language LoRA, the skill residuals, the router, and the shared action projections and time MLP are updated; every primitive is held frozen, so the base per-skill action-expert adapters are preserved by construction. On RoboCasa365, PRISM achieves 56.43% atomic-skill success and reaches 20.00% on long-horizon composite tasks, while a standard $π_{0.5}$-LoRA two-stage fine-tune reaches 17.86% atomic and 17.50% composite success. We additionally validate PRISM on an AgileX PIPER real-robot setup.

title: ActPrune: Action-Grounded Visual Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models perform versatile manipulation tasks from language instructions, but their inference cost limits how fast a robot can respond in closed-loop control.

extra.full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models perform versatile manipulation tasks from language instructions, but their inference cost limits how fast a robot can respond in closed-loop control. Visual token pruning reduces this cost; however, prior methods estimate token redundancy from encoded visual embeddings or attention, only after the visual encoder has processed the entire observation. We propose \ours, a training-free token pruning method that moves the pruning decision ahead of the vision encoder by grounding it in a geometric prior derived from the robot's own action. The action chunk predicted at the previous control step is already available before the current observation is encoded, and it specifies the end-effector and camera motion between consecutive observations. The same action affects the two standard camera views asymmetrically: in the fixed third-person view, \ours retains patches along the projected end-effector trajectory together with semantic anchors, while in the wrist view, it prunes patches that remain unchanged after compensating for the action-induced camera motion. Extensive experiments on two simulation environments (LIBERO and VLABench) and four real-robot tasks demonstrate that \ours achieves up to 1.61 $\times$ speedup and 59.5\% FLOPs reduction with negligible degradation in success rates.

title: Agibot: An Open-Source Modular Swerve-Drive Robot Platform for Agricultural Robotics Research and Education
summary: Agricultural production faces persistent labor shortages and increasing demand for automation, yet progress in agricultural robotics remains constrained by the limited availability of affordable, flexible, and accessible research platforms.

extra.comment: 14 pages. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on AgriFood Electronics (TAFE)
extra.full_text: Agricultural production faces persistent labor shortages and increasing demand for automation, yet progress in agricultural robotics remains constrained by the limited availability of affordable, flexible, and accessible research platforms. This paper presents Agibot, an open-source, modular, low-cost agricultural robotics platform designed for autonomy research and experimentation, with potential applications in hands-on robotics education. The platform integrates four-wheel independent swerve drive, swappable computing, distributed embedded control, multimodal sensing, and configurable manipulation within a unified sense-plan-act-verify framework supporting perception, control, navigation, manipulation, and autonomous task verification. The platform was evaluated through representative row-crop navigation and manipulation tasks under varying lighting and soil conditions. Experiments demonstrated reliable lane following, autonomous row-to-row navigation, target identification, seed dispensing, plant manipulation, and closed-loop verification of task success. Its modular architecture supports independent testing, modification, and validation of autonomy components for rapid prototyping and experimentation. These proof-of-concept tasks, controller-tuning studies, and integrated trials demonstrate the platform's research capabilities, while its accessible and reconfigurable design supports its use for hands-on robotics education. By combining affordability, modularity, open-source accessibility, configurable manipulation, and end-to-end sense-plan-act-verify autonomy, Agibot provides a practical platform for agricultural robotics research, technology development, and workforce training.

title: Lodos: A Lightweight Simulator Designed for Contact-Rich Interactions with Detailed Meshes
summary: In recent years, massively parallelized rigid-body simulation has played a central role in robotics research, enabling rapid progress in areas such as reinforcement learning, stochastic optimal control, and randomized smoothing-based trajectory optimization.

extra.full_text: In recent years, massively parallelized rigid-body simulation has played a central role in robotics research, enabling rapid progress in areas such as reinforcement learning, stochastic optimal control, and randomized smoothing-based trajectory optimization. Particularly in contact-rich settings, the scalability of such simulations in large part depends on well-optimized representations of collision geometry, often requiring a coarse approximation of the underlying surfaces using primitives such as spheres, capsules, cylinders, and boxes. Whenever the complexity of the surfaces or the precision demands of the application render such approximations insufficient, it is instead necessary to employ mesh-mesh collisions, which impose a significant reduction in throughput. This paper proposes a simulation framework designed from scratch to address this bottleneck, with novel routines for broadphase and narrowphase collision detection as well as the subsequent contact dynamics computation. As experimentally validated, the framework matches existing well-established simulators in terms of physical faithfulness, and can achieve approximately an order of magnitude higher throughput in the detailed mesh-mesh collision setting that it specializes in. The source code is available at https://github.com/martius-lab/lodos.

title: CPNav: Calibrated Vision-Language Navigation for Object-Goal Search in Unseen Environments
summary: Directing a robot to locate a target object in unseen environments remains a central challenge in embodied AI. Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based methods provide rich semantic reasoning but often produce uncalibrated and overconfident action decisions.

extra.full_text: Directing a robot to locate a target object in unseen environments remains a central challenge in embodied AI. Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based methods provide rich semantic reasoning but often produce uncalibrated and overconfident action decisions. We introduce CPNav, a navigation framework that combines collision-aware planning with statistically calibrated VLM action scoring for map-free object-goal navigation. From RGB-D input, CPNav constructs a navigability map, generates collision-free motion primitives, and queries two VLMs for goal detection and action scoring. The resulting scores are calibrated offline via conformal prediction (CP) using oracle actions obtained through a tree-structured exploration procedure with backtracking, providing finite-sample guarantees at a user-specified risk level. The CP layer is model-agnostic and can wrap any VLM policy. Online, calibrated VLM scores guide action selection, while a tree-structured exploration history records alternative actions and allows backtracking. We evaluate CPNav in both simulation and real-world hardware settings. In AI Habitat simulation, compared with the uncalibrated baseline method, CPNav achieves relative SR and SPL improvements of 6.2% and 11.4% on HM3D v0.2, and 12.4% and 8.8% on MP3D, respectively. In real-world deployment on a modified Hiwonder MentorPi robot, the corresponding improvements in SR and SPL are 24.9% and 15.2%, respectively. Code is available at https://github.com/practice-lab-ucla/CPnav.

title: Coding or Cheating? An Investigation of Frontier Coding LLMs
summary: Frontier agentic LLMs are trained on verifiable rewards in reinforcement learning (RL) environments built from real software repositories. A passing test suite is treated as the reward for solving the task. We show that, on hard problems, frontier models often satisfy these rewards by obtaining the answer instead of deriving it, known as reward hacking.

extra.full_text: Frontier agentic LLMs are trained on verifiable rewards in reinforcement learning (RL) environments built from real software repositories. A passing test suite is treated as the reward for solving the task. We show that, on hard problems, frontier models often satisfy these rewards by obtaining the answer instead of deriving it, known as reward hacking. Prior reports document this behavior on public benchmarks. We test its persistence on unseen problems.   In a hardened environment where the answer cannot leak, nearly every model we tested attempted to recover the answer, escalating through tiers of increasingly specialized exploitation: mining the repository history for the upstream fix, inspecting the git object store directly, and sweeping the filesystem for a possible newer copy of the source or hidden tests. These attempts were concentrated on the hardest problems, and the models differed in whether, how often, and how deeply they escalated. Our position is that this behavior is a learned shortcut, acquired in RL environments that leak the answer, not a sign of intelligence. We release agent traces for these models to support further study at https://huggingface.co/datasets/logitly-ai/reward-hacking-raw-v1.

title: Jais 3: Introducing Arabic-centric Agentic AI
summary: We present Jais 3, a fleet of six open, Arabic-centric agentic language models ranging from 0.9B to 375B parameters.
authors: Sheikh Khalid bin Khalifa Al Nahyan

extra.full_text: We present Jais 3, a fleet of six open, Arabic-centric agentic language models ranging from 0.9B to 375B parameters. Jais 3 is built to complete tasks for Arabic speakers, not only to answer questions in plain text: it is trained to plan multi-step tasks, call tools and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, operate a terminal, search the web, and read, edit, and produce PDF, spreadsheet, and presentation files, while communicating with the user in Arabic. Instead of pretraining from scratch, we adapt each model of the fully open K2 Horizon fleet to Arabic through continual pretraining, followed by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), final token preference optimization (FTPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We combine natural Arabic text with translated, transliterated, and synthetic Arabic, and replay the base model's own training data to keep its reasoning, agentic, and English abilities. Jais 3 covers Modern Standard Arabic and the major regional dialects, follows instructions with Arabic-specific constraints, and inherits the 512K-token context window of K2 Horizon (all models except the 0.9B). To our knowledge, its 375B model is the largest open Arabic-centric language model to date. title: Designing Effective Monitor-Based Interventions for Mitigating Reward Hacking During RL
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) rewards are notoriously difficult to design and control, often leading to the model learning unintended behaviors such as reward hacking.

extra.full_text: Reinforcement learning (RL) rewards are notoriously difficult to design and control, often leading to the model learning unintended behaviors such as reward hacking. One potential solution is to monitor for reward hacking and penalize it when detected; however, training against a monitor could lead to evasive behavior, and our general understanding of how to apply monitors effectively during training is limited. To study how best to use monitors to mitigate reward hacking, we introduce and open source three realistic environments where Qwen3-4B reward hacks: a coding environment hackable via test overwriting, a medical chat environment hackable via sycophancy, and a biography generation environment hackable via hallucination. We first focus on the coding environment, where we find that: (1) models can learn to evade highly accurate monitors by exploiting systemic flaws in probes and LLM judges; (2) monitors that leak more learning signal during RL suppress reward hacking but are more often evaded; and (3) including easier problems in training can decrease reward hacking. We apply our findings to build better reward hacking monitors for the medical chat and biography generation environments that improve upon naive baselines to reduce reward hacking rates across seeds to before-training levels in some interventions. Our results demonstrate that our takeaways translate to new settings and that better monitor intervention designs are possible.

title: PLS-GS: Probabilistic Lidar Scaffolds for Compact, Surface-Aligned Gaussian Splatting
summary: While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is typically optimized from images only, many robotics and mapping applications provide both camera and high-definition LiDAR data, combining rich visual appearance with accurate geometric structure.

extra.comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. Main paper and supplementary material. Code: https://github.com/k-harikumar/PLS-GS
extra.full_text: While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is typically optimized from images only, many robotics and mapping applications provide both camera and high-definition LiDAR data, combining rich visual appearance with accurate geometric structure. We introduce PLS-GS, a probabilistic LiDAR scaffold for Gaussian Splatting that exploits this complementary sensing setting to construct a compact 3DGS representation aligned to the measured surface. PLS-GS fits a Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Model jointly over position and color, yielding a continuous and adaptive scaffold that eliminates the need for discrete scene partitioning such as voxel grids or octrees. The fitted mixture then guides the renderable 3DGS Gaussians: each rendering Gaussian is associated with a GMM component and constrained in the local surface frame induced by that component's covariance. A Mahalanobis support loss bounds the deviation of the rendering Gaussians from the corresponding LiDAR-derived surface. Across five large outdoor scenes, PLS-GS places primitives markedly closer to the LiDAR measurements than both image- and LiDAR-initialized baselines, while employing substantially fewer primitives, yielding a considerably more compact model and faster rendering. At matched capacity, PLS-GS places primitives closer to the LiDAR measurements, with comparable rendering quality. Code is available at https://github.com/k-harikumar/PLS-GS.

title: RigidGS: Geometry-Aware Object Decoupling for Rigid-Body Interaction in 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Interactive VR/MR applications demand photorealistic 3D representations that support real-time rendering and object-level manipulation. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) achieves high rendering quality, it represents scenes as unstructured, monolithic primitives.

extra.comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Accepted at WACV 2027 (Applications Track). Project page: https://gyreyirisansah.github.io/rigidgs
extra.full_text: Interactive VR/MR applications demand photorealistic 3D representations that support real-time rendering and object-level manipulation. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) achieves high rendering quality, it represents scenes as unstructured, monolithic primitives. Existing object-aware 3DGS methods jointly optimize geometry and semantic states but suffer from two key failure modes: noisy foundation-model masks on complex geometry, and label-geometry coupling, in which co-optimized identity gradients mislabel boundary Gaussians. We introduce RigidGS, an end-to-end pipeline that decouples geometric learning from object identity. We propose a depth- and temporally-aware mask refinement module that addresses two complementary SAM2 failures: over-inclusion on thin structures and under-inclusion on multimodal-depth objects. We then determine object identities entirely upstream via COLMAP projection voting and freeze them during training, directing mask supervision solely toward geometric optimization. Refined masks alone substantially improve competing methods, yet a residual gap in label-geometry coupling persists that our fixed-identity design eliminates. RigidGS outperforms prior object-aware 3DGS methods on LLFF/NVOS, Mip-NeRF~360, and iNeRF360, improving segmentation and boundary IoU by 7.7 and 14.5 points on LLFF/NVOS. Finally, RigidGS enables real-time rigid-body manipulation on Meta Quest~2 without mesh extraction. Our code and project page are available at https://gyreyirisansah.github.io/rigidgs.

title: ATLAS: A Multi-Procedure Benchmark and Context-Aware Model for Surgical Anatomy Segmentation
summary: Recognizing anatomical structures during minimally invasive surgery (MIS) could support intraoperative navigation and improve patient safety, but progress is limited by small, single-procedure datasets and by segmentation methods developed for natural scenes. This work addresses both limitations through a new dataset and model.
authors: Ronald L. P. D. de Jong

extra.full_text: Recognizing anatomical structures during minimally invasive surgery (MIS) could support intraoperative navigation and improve patient safety, but progress is limited by small, single-procedure datasets and by segmentation methods developed for natural scenes. This work addresses both limitations through a new dataset and model. First, we introduce ATLAS-120k, a clip-level semantic segmentation dataset of 121,018 annotated frames from 100 surgical videos, covering 14 laparoscopic and robot-assisted procedures and 41 classes. Annotations were created with a pipeline that combines manual labeling, tracker-based propagation, and review by surgeons. Second, we propose ATLAS (Anatomy Recognition with Context Learning using Foundation Representations), a video semantic segmentation model for surgical anatomy recognition. ATLAS builds on in-domain foundation-model embeddings and adds context queries for the procedure and surgical phase, together with query propagation between frames for short-term memory. ATLAS outperforms state-of-the-art natural-image and in-domain foundation models in both segmentation accuracy and temporal consistency, achieving a Dice score of 0.70 with ViT-L while running in real time at 76.2 FPS. Ablations show that the context queries improve accuracy and that query propagation improves temporal consistency. ATLAS also generalizes well, matching a dedicated model zero-shot on CholecSeg8k and improving phase recognition on AutoLaparo over SurgeNet initialization. The model weights, dataset annotations, and annotation tool are publicly available at https://github.com/TimJaspers0801/ATLAS.

title: Are Drone Ports the Next Annoying Tech Neighbor?
summary: Rick and Marcia LeCompte loved to watch the Cooper’s hawks that frequented a sweet-gum tree in their yard in Baton Rouge, La. But this October, the hawks were gone. Marcia LeCompte is convinced the birds were scared away by the same flying robots that have been vexing the couple since early September.

extra.full_text: Rick and Marcia LeCompte loved to watch the Cooper’s hawks that frequented a sweet-gum tree in their yard in Baton Rouge, La. But this October, the hawks were gone. Marcia LeCompte is convinced the birds were scared away by the same flying robots that have been vexing the couple since early September. The noise had them spending less time outside in their garden, and even inside their home, they couldn’t escape the near-constant buzzing. Angry and feeling harassed, the LeComptes began to think about moving. The problem: delivery drones. Amazon’s MK30 delivery drones are large and must fly near the ground when making deliveries. Annabel Lee-Ellis/Press Association/AP Images Last August, Amazon Prime Air began flying its MK30 drones from a distribution center 3.2 kilometers (2 miles) from the LeComptes’ home. People in the neighborhood first noticed just a few of the drones, flying high (U.S. regulations authorize drones to fly at up to 120 meters (400 feet )). But a couple of weeks later, they felt as if drones were everywhere, and often flying much lower. The high-pitched whine of rotors was what bothered them the most, says Blake Fugler, who lives in the same neighborhood. It sounded as if a neighbor was constantly using a weed whacker for hours every day, he says. Acoustic research has found that the noise of drone rotors is more annoying than that of cars, airplanes, and other familiar background sounds. Once flights became frequent, the noise made people miserable. “Outside the house on a Saturday between 9 and 10 a.m., I counted a drone every 48 seconds,” says Fugler’s partner, Cristina Boone. Delivery Drone Concerns Neighbors had concerns about drones buzzing over playgrounds, schools, and services at the local cemetery; a drone that made a forced landing on the median of a busy highway; and the fact that drones are equipped with cameras. Then word spread about Amazon’s plans as reported in the FAA’s Environmental Assessment for the facility : “Operations would occur between 6 a.m. and 10:30 p.m., with 100 of the 1,000 daily delivery operations (10%) occurring during the period from 6 a.m. to 7 a.m. and 10 p.m. to 10:30 p.m.” As they quickly expand their operations around the world, delivery-drone companies—including Alphabet’s Wing Aviation , Amazon Prime Air , Doordash Air , JD Logistics , Manna Aero , Matternet , Meituan , Zipline , and more, say their flying robots are quiet , safe , and unobtrusive . Massive expansion is planned for the near future. In Asia, for example, Meituan launched its latest “low-altitude delivery network’’ in September in Shanghai , while JD continues to expand drone service in rural China . In the U.S., Zipline and Uber have announced a partnership with the goal of 1 million drone deliveries a day by the end of 2029. Wing aims to have 270 U.S. drone hubs operating by the end of 2027 . And Amazon Prime Air, which currently delivers in about 85 municipalities in the U.S., says it plans to serve 500 by the end of 2026. A Wing “nest” of delivery drones in a parking lot. Wing Yet as the companies aggressively scale up, “the public outreach piece has probably been more of an afterthought than it should have been,” says David Ison , a specialist in Emerging Aviation Technologies and Land Use Compatibility at the Washington State Department of Transportation, who has worked on the state’s drone-hub land-use guidelines. “I think what companies assumed is everybody would be cheering that they could get things delivered by drone in half an hour.” Companies tout drone delivery as a way to do good. Zipline has delivered blood plasma and vaccines in Africa . Material that Wing provided at public meetings in the Dallas Fort Worth area says its deliveries there have saved more than 1,000 tonnes of carbon that would have been emitted by delivery trucks. For businesses, drone delivery is supposed to offer faster service and reduce costs, although whether drones are actually less costly is a complex question that depends on a variety of interconnected factors . The commercial and philanthropic use cases make for an unusual sales pitch, notes Ison. “It’s a lot easier argument to make when you’re saying you’re delivering blood to an accident site than when you’re delivering a fidget toy.” But instead of being impressed, people troubled by drones say they feel they’re being pushed around by a distant corporation. “It’s the same way data centers strong-arm communities,” says Boone. Newly arrived drone launch sites have triggered similar fears from China to France to Australia to within many communities in the United States, including suburban Detroit ; Richardson, Texas ; Glendale, Ariz .; East Cobb, Ga .; Maplewood, Mo .; and Westborough, Mass . The response has sometimes been enough to shut down local drone operations completely. An early Wing trial in 2018 in suburban Canberra, Australia, shut down a few months later, after activists formed an opposition group and rallied support in Parliament . In response, the company “fundamentally reshaped [its] engineering priorities, flight operations, and community-engagement strategy,” says Jessie Poole-Strang, Wing’s communications lead. It redesigned its drones to reduce noise, changed flight-path algorithms, and now makes efforts to familiarize people with its robots before a facility opens. Communities Take Action Still, legal and political campaigns against drones continue to arise. On 28 September, 15 U.S. states and Harris County, Texas, sued the FAA to stop it from easing its environmental assessment rules for drone sites, which are key to local government control. In April, the Cobb County Board of Commissioners in Georgia denied a zoning request for a Wing drone facility there. In response to the Cobb County complaints, a Wing spokesperson said the company was hearing “positive feedback” from people in Cobb County. Similarly, Amazon representatives have said most feedback from customers about drone delivery is “ overwhelmingly positive ,” and Zipline has encouraged at least one local official to refer to drone delivery as a “totally normal part of life.” Wing’s drone is smaller and lighter than some other delivery drones. Wing But fundamental concerns remain. “There are safety, noise, and visual-pollution issues with all these platforms,” Ison says, noting that it’s important not to lump all drone technologies together. For example, concerns about accidents are more relevant to Amazon’s MK-30 drone, which weighs almost 36 kilograms (80 pounds) , than to Wing’s largest drone, which weighs less than 11 kilograms (25 pounds) with its payload included . Another safety consideration: Wing and Zipline , he notes, lower their packages to the ground via a tether, which leaves the craft higher in the air than Amazon’s , which must get low enough to drop its load without damage. And Ison expects continuing disputes about noise. This is because U.S. law is not settled on people’s rights to airspace just above their property. “Maybe someone says, ‘You can’t fly over my house’ or ‘I want you to pay me to fly over my house,’ ” Ison says. “That is a murky area that is going to have to be worked out in court.” For now, in the Baton Rouge neighborhood where the LeComptes, Fugler, and Boone live, the skies have calmed. Their councilman says Amazon Prime Air has responded to the outcry by rerouting 70 percent of drone flights elsewhere, although since the drones are not allowed to fly over highways, that likely means other residential neighborhoods. As of late October, LeCompte says she is now seeing, “two or three a day” over their home, although on a trip to the bank a few miles away, she counted eight in 20 minutes. “Sorry for those folks, but I thank Amazon for clearing our sky.”
